claims.text: An adjusted synthesis condition can minimize the time gap between reduction events of different noble-metal precursors.
Synchronizing precursor reduction forces simultaneous nucleation.
Simultaneous nucleation statistically favors a random, single-phase HEA nanoparticle.
Standard procedures exhibit sequential reduction tendencies among different noble-metal precursors.
The starting material is a homogeneous, solid, single-source mixture containing five noble-metal salts with limited atomic mobility.
Low-temperature solid or mixed-precursor conditions restrict free-atom mobility.
Restricted-mobility conditions ensure that nucleation events occur nearly simultaneously.
Rapid, synchronized formation of metal atoms produces spatially uniform nucleation.
Uniform nucleation minimizes elemental segregation and prevents phase-segregated or intermetallic domains.
Synchronizing reduction minimizes the opportunity for one metal to nucleate separately and forces concurrent deposition of all metals.
High supersaturation of diverse metal atoms promotes stochastic mixing.
Stochastic mixing yields a random alloy rather than phase separation caused by sequential reduction.
The synchronized condition will produce nanoparticles with a uniform elemental distribution and a single-phase HEA structure.
An unsynchronized baseline synthesis is expected to produce phase-separated or compositionally heterogeneous nanoparticles.
Differences in precursor redox potentials produce sequential reduction in the conventional baseline.
The proposed synchronization mechanism applies to noble-metal systems under low-temperature, solid or mixed-precursor conditions with limited mobility.
The mechanism may not apply to high-mobility solution syntheses or systems dominated by thermodynamic rather than kinetic effects.
In situ XRD, multi-edge XAS, and STEM-EDS can jointly assess phase state, reduction sequence, and nanoscale elemental uniformity.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits temperature ramping as the manipulated condition, while the experimental design says temperature must remain identical between groups. Those requirements are incompatible if temperature ramping is selected.

These fields broadly associate consecutive or unsynchronized reduction with phase separation, but one cited comparative record explicitly reports that five-element single-phase HEA particles formed even when the elements reduced consecutively. The hypothesis does not reconcile that exception with its proposed governing role for synchronization.
